content.name: p
children: An auditor asks a harder question than “what grants are in our YAML?”:

children.name: strong
children: can this role actually perform the operation?
Acme’s role graph is tidy, but PostgreSQL has access paths outside ordinary named ACLs.

content.name: h2
children: Close the PUBLIC path explicitly

content.name: p
children: PostgreSQL gives

children.name: code
children: PUBLIC
—every role—

children.name: code
children: EXECUTE
on new functions by default. State both desired absences so existing and future functions converge:

content.name: Fence
children:
grants:
  - role: PUBLIC
    ensure: absent
    privileges: [EXECUTE]
    object: { type: function, schema: billing_api, name: "*" }

default_privileges:
  - owner: app_owner
    scope: { type: global }
    grant:
      - role: PUBLIC
        ensure: absent
        privileges: [EXECUTE]
        on_type: function

content.name: p
children: The global default matters because PostgreSQL’s built-in function default is global. A schema-scoped revoke cannot subtract a global grant.

content.name: h2
children: Keep the other two boundaries visible

content.name: p
children: A

children.name: code
children: SECURITY DEFINER
function is an intentional privilege boundary. Review its owner, body, fixed

children.name: code
children: search_path
, callable surface, and

children.name: code
children: PUBLIC
exposure. pgroles manages who may execute the function; it does not prove the function body is safe.

content.name: p

children.name: code
children: WITH GRANT OPTION

lets an application grantee delegate an object privilege. pgroles checks whether its executor can grant wildcard privileges safely, but it does not model or converge grant options held by application roles. Audit and manage that boundary separately.

children.name: strong
children: Desired ACLs are necessary; effective-access tests tell you whether every other path agrees with them.
